issues.legal_issue: A petition invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction is maintainable against a National Commission order made in an appeal from a State Commission when no further statutory appeal is provided against that kind of order.
material_facts: The National Commission decided an appeal from an order of a State Commission and affirmed that order.
The governing appeal provision to the Supreme Court covered specified kinds of National Commission orders but not orders made in appeals from State Commission decisions.
The respondent challenged the National Commission’s appellate order before the High Court under its supervisory jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could entertain the petition, and its decision to do so was correct.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 58(1)(a)(iii) and 67 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provide for appeals from State Commission orders to the National Commission, but provide a further appeal to the Supreme Court only for National Commission orders made under Section 58(1)(a)(i) or (ii). The National Commission is a statutory tribunal exercising judicial power and is subject to the High Court’s jurisdiction under Article 227. Associated Cement Companies Limited v. P.N. Sharma establishes the relevant test for a tribunal; L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India holds that High Court judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 cannot wholly be excluded; and State of Karnataka v. Vishwabarathi House Building Co-operative Society recognizes the availability of High Court review of consumer commission orders.

predicates.consumer_appeal_from_state_commission: A consumer dispute is decided by a State Commission and its decision is appealed to the National Commission.
predicates.statutory_tribunal_decides_dispute: A body empowered by statute determines the rights of parties to a dispute by applying law to the relevant facts.
predicates.no_further_statutory_appeal: The governing law provides no further statutory appeal against the kind of order being challenged.

issues.definition: When a statutory tribunal decides a consumer appeal from a State Commission and no further statutory appeal is available, a petition invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: When considering interim relief against a tribunal’s order in a supervisory petition, the High Court must remain within the limited scope of its supervisory jurisdiction.
material_facts: The High Court entertained a supervisory petition challenging the National Commission’s appellate order and stayed that order pending further proceedings.
The Supreme Court left the merits of the dispute for the High Court but directed it to bear in mind the limited nature of supervisory jurisdiction when considering interim relief.
issues.conclusion: Any interim stay or other interim relief granted in such a petition is subject to the limits governing the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers a limited power of superintendence, and the High Court must exercise it within its established parameters, including when considering interim relief. The Court relied on Estralla Rubber v. Dass Estate (P) Ltd. and Garment Craft v. Prakash Chand Goel for the scope and limits of Article 227 jurisdiction.

predicates.supervisory_petition_challenges_tribunal: A party brings a petition invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction to challenge an order of a tribunal.
predicates.interim_relief_is_considered: The High Court considers whether to grant temporary relief while the petition is pending.

issues.definition: If interim relief is considered in a supervisory petition challenging a tribunal order, that relief must remain within the limits of the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
